prompt: Which are the first four stages of the customer acquisition funnel?
explanation: The six-step acquisition funnel: awareness → interest → consideration → intent → evaluation → purchase. AIDA is a different (communication) model. Past exam question.

prompt: Which statements about customer acquisition cost (CAC) are true?
explanation: CAC = marketing costs / customers acquired, calculated for a specific campaign or time window – so it has a time reference. Past exam question.

prompt: Why is customer acquisition important for a business?

options.text: It generates money to meet costs, pay employees and reinvest in growth
It shows evidence of traction to investors, partners and influencers
Acquisition costs have decreased strongly in recent years
It replaces the need for customer retention

explanation: The cost of acquiring customers increased by over 50% in five years (HubSpot) – which makes measuring CAC and CLV crucial.

prompt: Which tools can be used to acquire customers?
explanation: Referrals and SEO drive new customers directly; social listening helps identify and engage prospects. Past exam question.

prompt: Which statements describe the three product levels?

options.text: Core product – satisfies the central underlying need ("a customer buys a three-inch hole, not a drill bit")
Tangible product – features, styling, quality, brand name, packaging
Augmented product – additional services and features that enhance the experience
Core product – the warranty and installation services

explanation: Warranties and installation are service attributes that augment the product.

prompt: Which belong to the SYMBOLIC attributes in the product component model?
explanation: Repair, maintenance, warranties, installation, financing, spare parts and deliveries are service attributes.

prompt: In the customer value equation, which are COSTS?
explanation: Value = benefits (functional, psychological, economic) − costs (monetary, perceived risk, inconvenience).

prompt: Which are objective measures of customer value?
explanation: Focus groups, direct survey questions and importance ratings are perceptual, unconstrained measures.

prompt: Which measures of customer value are PERCEPTUAL?
explanation: Choice models (e.g. multinomial logit) and data mining are behavioural measures – they use past behaviour.

prompt: Which are limitations of importance ratings?

options.text: Respondents can rate everything as very important
No trade-offs, so willingness to pay is hard to determine
Rated items often do not drive actual choice behaviour

explanation: Importance ratings are unconstrained; they do not need past purchase data.

prompt: Which statements on the comparison of customer value measures are correct (Lilien et al.)?

options.text: Objective value measures are very costly per respondent but deliver very high insight
Behavioural value measures need past purchase data
Behavioural measures work well for lead users and in dynamic, changing markets
Unconstrained perceived measures are cheap but have low predictive power

explanation: Behavioural measures need past purchase data and are NOT good in dynamic markets or for lead users.

prompt: What is the annual cost of the incumbent chips for ESCP?
explanation: ESCP pays 6 € per chip and replaces 400 chips twice a year. The supplier margin is irrelevant for the customer's cost.

prompt: Which of the following is the VIU for the new chips (without shutdown costs)?
explanation: The new chip lasts a full year and replaces two old chips: 2 × 6 € = 12 €. The supplier's margins are distractors.

prompt: Which of the following is the shutdown cost for the OLD chips per year?
explanation: Old chips: maintenance every 6 months → 2 shutdowns × 1,000 € = 2,000 € per year – not among the options.

prompt: Which of the following is the shutdown cost for the NEW chips per year?
explanation: New chips: maintenance every 12 months → 1 shutdown × 1,000 € = 1,000 € per year.

prompt: Which of the following is the VIU for the new chips, including shutdown costs?
explanation: Shutdown savings = 2,000 € − 1,000 € = 1,000 € per year, spread over 400 new chips = 2.50 € per chip. VIU = 12 € + 2.50 € = 14.50 €. Check: old total 4,800 + 2,000 = 6,800 € = 400 × VIU + 1,000 → VIU = 14.50 €.

prompt: The lowest price ESCP can get for the new chips is 14 € per chip. What do you recommend, based on the VIU including shutdown costs?

options.text: Purchase the new technology of chips
Do NOT purchase the new technology of chips
You cannot give a sufficient answer based on your calculations

explanation: VIU (14.50 €) is the maximum willingness to pay; the price (14 €) is below it, so ESCP saves 0.50 € per chip.

prompt: Now assume that the shutdown costs increase from 1,000 € to 1,200 €. How does this affect the VIU of the new chips?

options.text: No proper answer is possible, based on the data
VIU will decrease, and ESCP should not purchase the new chips
VIU will increase, but not enough to justify the price per chip
VIU will increase, so that ESCP should purchase the new chips

prompt: What is the VIU of the Y-rings without shutdown costs?
explanation: One Y-ring replaces two Z-rings: 2 × 8 € = 16 €.

prompt: What is the VIU of the Y-rings including shutdown costs of 3,000 € per shutdown?
explanation: Z-rings: 4 shutdowns × 3,000 = 12,000 €/year; Y-rings: 2 shutdowns = 6,000 €. Savings 6,000 € over 500 Y-rings per year (250 × 2) = 12 € per ring. VIU = 16 + 12 = 28 €.

prompt: Which statements on the two website versions are correct?

options.text: Version A has the higher click-through rate
Version B has the higher conversion rate
Version B has the lower ad cost per sale
Version A has the higher return on ad investment

prompt: In hypothesis testing, which statements about errors are correct?

options.text: A type I error (α) means rejecting H0 although it is correct
A type II error (β) means not rejecting H0 although it is incorrect
A test can control both errors simultaneously
Usually α is fixed (e.g. 5% in social sciences) and a test minimising β is used

explanation: A test cannot control both errors at the same time.

prompt: Which KPI and test fit together in the sustainable t-shirt A/B test?

options.text: Willingness to buy – chi-square goodness-of-fit test

explanation: The t-test compares the means of two groups; the chi-square test compares observed vs expected frequencies (test of independence).

prompt: Which are benefits of A/B testing?

options.text: It never requires a control group

explanation: The control (A) is the existing version; the challenger (B) is the variation.

statement: CAC = marketing costs associated with a campaign / number of customers acquired from that campaign.
explanation: For an accurate CAC include all marketing-related costs (campaign spend, salaries, …).

statement: For marketers, services such as concerts or MBA programmes can also be products.
explanation: A product is anything offered for attention, acquisition, use or consumption that might satisfy a want or need.

statement: "In the factory we make cosmetics; in the store we sell hope" (Revlon) illustrates the augmented product.
explanation: It illustrates the CORE product – the underlying need or benefit.

statement: In the new product development process, testing includes pre-test and pre-launch forecasting and test marketing.
explanation: NPDP: opportunity identification → design → testing → introduction → life cycle management, with GO/NO decisions.

statement: Toyota's Lexus succeeded by offering European-style benefits at a price advantage and reduced perceived risk.
explanation: Benefits: engineering, safety, style, fit, finish. Costs: lower price than Mercedes, reduced perceived risk.

statement: Value-in-use can be calculated as the maximum willingness to pay for a focal product, given a reference product.
explanation: Reference: e.g. the previous product version or the most important competitor.

statement: Indirect survey questions focus on the worth of the entire product offering.
explanation: They focus on CHANGES ("If we could increase the life of your cartridges by 20%, how much would it be worth to you?").

statement: Focus groups bring five to ten customers together with a trained moderator; groupthink can lead to homogeneous results.
explanation: They aim to understand shared perceptions of a well-defined target group.

statement: Conjoint analysis is a constrained perceptual measure of customer value.
explanation: Respondents rate systematically varied offerings, which forces trade-offs.

statement: Benchmarking asks respondents how much more (or less) they would pay if features were added to (or removed from) a benchmark offering.
explanation: It determines willingness to pay per attribute.

statement: The multinomial logit model states that the purchase probability of brand A equals A's perceived benefit divided by the sum of perceived benefits of all brands.
explanation: A simple and powerful behavioural choice model.

statement: Inferential statistics draws conclusions about a population based on a sample.
explanation: Two goals: estimation and hypothesis testing.

statement: The null hypothesis H0 is the hypothesis of an effect.
explanation: H0 is the hypothesis of NO effect; H1 is the hypothesised effect. The aim of a test is to reject H0.

statement: In an A/B test, the existing design is the control (version A) and the new design the challenger (version B).
explanation: Ideally the same share of visitors sees each version.

statement: Testing different product photos or where shipping costs are displayed can lower shopping cart abandonment.
explanation: 40–75% of e-commerce customers leave items in their cart.

statement: Google and Facebook routinely divert a fraction of users, without telling them, to slightly different page versions and compare their behaviour.
explanation: A/B testing turns design questions into data-driven matters – discussed in the context of surveillance capitalism.

statement: You want to know if the design of your rebranded newsletter generates a higher click-through rate than your old newsletter.
explanation: Two versions of the same element, one KPI → classic A/B test.

statement: You want to know if your female customers are more likely to buy your new t-shirt than male customers are to buy your new shoes.
explanation: You compare different products AND different groups – not two versions of one element. Likelihood across customer characteristics calls for regression, not an A/B test.

statement: You want to know if changing your checkout button colour from grey to dark blue increases the share of people who proceed with checkout.
explanation: One element varied, randomised split, conversion as KPI.

statement: The new chips should be bought at 14 € because their VIU including shutdown costs is 14.50 €.
explanation: Price below VIU → value for ESCP.

statement: A purchase price of 25 € per Y-ring is justified when shutdown costs are considered.
explanation: VIU incl. shutdowns = 28 € > 25 €. Without shutdowns (VIU 16 €) it would not be.

prompt: Determine the VIU of the Y-rings (a) without and (b) with shutdown costs of 3,000 € per shutdown. Show your calculations.
modelAnswer:
a) Z-rings are changed 4× per year → 4 × 8 € = 32 € per ring position and year. A Y-ring lasts twice as long (changed 2× per year), so one Y-ring replaces two Z-rings: VIU = 2 × 8 € = 16 €.
b) Annual cost with Z-rings: 250 × 4 × 8 € = 8,000 € + 4 shutdowns × 3,000 € = 12,000 € → 20,000 €. With Y-rings: 250 × 2 × VIU + 2 × 3,000 € = 500 × VIU + 6,000 €. Indifference: 500 × VIU + 6,000 = 20,000 → VIU = 28 €.
keyPoints: Z-ring shutdown costs 12,000 € vs Y-ring 6,000 € per year

prompt: Explain the (high) difference between the two VIU results and whether a price of 25 € per Y-ring justifies a purchase.
modelAnswer: The first VIU only reflects the material cost replaced by the longer lifespan (2 × 8 € = 16 €). The second VIU also includes the downtime costs avoided: each extra shutdown costs 3,000 €, far more than the rings themselves, so halving the number of shutdowns adds 12 € of value per ring (28 €). At 25 € the purchase is justified: the price is below the maximum willingness to pay of 28 €, saving 3 € per ring (1,500 € per year). Without counting shutdowns, 25 € would look too expensive – showing why VIU must include all usage costs.
keyPoints: Second VIU includes avoided shutdown costs (28 €)
Shutdown costs are large relative to ring price

prompt: Calculate click-through rate, conversion rate, ad cost per sale and return on ad investment for both website versions. Which one performs better?
modelAnswer:
A: CTR = 1,298/20,000 = 6.49%; conversion = 75/20,000 = 0.375%; cost per sale = 1,800/75 = 24.00 €; revenue = 75 × 108 = 8,100 €; ROI = (8,100 − 1,800)/1,800 = 3.50 (350%).
B: CTR = 1,056/20,000 = 5.28%; conversion = 92/20,000 = 0.46%; cost per sale = 2,000/92 ≈ 21.74 €; revenue = 92 × 98 = 9,016 €; ROI = (9,016 − 2,000)/2,000 ≈ 3.51 (351%).
Version B performs (slightly) better on the bottom-line KPIs (conversion, cost per sale, ROI) although A generates more clicks.

prompt: Explain type I and type II errors and how a statistical test deals with them.
modelAnswer: A type I error (α) occurs when H0 is rejected although it is correct – we believe in an effect that does not exist. A type II error (β) occurs when H0 is not rejected although it is wrong – we miss an existing effect. A test cannot control both at the same time; therefore we fix the type I error at a threshold (usually 5% in social sciences) and use a test that minimises the type II error.
